 Home Alert Medicare beneficiaries are urged to review prescription drug plans before December 7 Medicare beneficiaries are urged to review prescription drug plans before December 7
 Sun, October 25, 2026 by Staff Report 
 SHARE NOW 
 Prescription pills drug prices cost 
 Medicare beneficiaries are being urged to review their prescription drug coverage during open enrollment to avoid unexpected costs and changes to their medications’ coverage in the coming year.
 Beneficiaries should not assume their current plans will remain unchanged – it’s incredibly important to look.
 The Medicare Part D open enrollment period runs from October 15 through December 7.
 Michael Day of Michael G. Day and Associates recommended reviewing options during November rather than waiting until the final weeks, when heavy website traffic can cause enrollment systems to slow down or crash. Play the full interview here:
 “The government system, you know, seems to crash early in the process as all the eager beavers jump on to do it,” Day said. “And then it tends to stabilize and run okay for a while, and in the last two weeks, you know, from late November through December 7, as the procrastinators then finally hit on it, that it starts crashing again.”
 Beneficiaries should use the enrollment period to compare available plans, even if they are satisfied with their current coverage.
 “Your plan is going to terminate on December 31. Period. No exceptions,” Day said. “And I don’t care that you like your plan. It’s gone, sayonara. It’s over, and so you must look at it again.”
 Failing to review coverage could lead to higher premiums, deductibles and copayments, as well as changes to the list of covered medications.
 Day described a client who did not want to review a current plan because the client was happy with it. He said the client needed to understand that the coverage and costs could change regardless of that satisfaction.
 He also cautioned against paying more than necessary for prescription drug coverage, particularly when a less expensive plan may cover the medications a beneficiary takes.
 “You need to pay attention to this thing,” Day said. “I don’t care that it covers everything. It’s covering everything’s dirt cheap anyway. You don’t need to pay $170 a month for this plan, so you need to go out and look and see what it’s covering.”
 Beneficiaries who need help comparing plans can seek assistance from professionals who understand the available options. Such assistance should focus on meeting a person’s needs rather than selling unrelated products.
 “It’s not an opportunity to sell people stuff that they didn’t go in to talk about,” Day said.
 It’s also important to review insurance coverage, estate-planning documents and preparations for long-term care.
 Day said his law office asks clients detailed questions because people sometimes take financial risks without realizing it.
 “Most people are engaged in behavior that they don’t realize is creating risk that they didn’t intend to take,” he said.
 The goal is to help clients protect themselves and avoid unnecessary risks, beginning with a review of their existing insurance and legal documents.
 “First things we want people to be secure,” Day said. “I haven’t encountered a client yet that isn’t interested in being secure, but a corollary to being secure is I want to avoid unnecessary risk.”
 Homeowners’ insurance policies, for example, may no longer reflect the cost of rebuilding a home after increases in construction costs.
 Some life insurance policyholders may be paying premiums without realizing their policies will not provide the expected death benefit.
 “Let me see the policies,” Day said, describing his approach to reviewing clients’ life insurance. He said he finds that about half of his clients have policies that will not pay a death benefit, even though they may not realize it.
 He also discussed the importance of reviewing auto insurance, umbrella liability coverage, health insurance, powers of attorney, wills and health care directives.
 Day cautioned that seemingly convenient estate-planning decisions, such as adding children’s names to bank accounts, can create unintended complications. Those arrangements could affect the inheritance of children with disabilities or substance abuse issues and potentially interfere with eligibility for government benefits.
 Long-term care planning also requires an individualized approach. Depending on a couple’s financial circumstances, the tax consequences of transferring retirement assets and the loss of pension income when a spouse enters a nursing home could make qualifying for government benefits financially difficult.
 In some circumstances, long-term care insurance may be a less expensive option, if the person qualifies for coverage.
 Day said the same insurance coverage is not necessarily appropriate for both spouses, and that planning should reflect their individual risks and financial situations.
 Medicare beneficiaries have until December 7 to review and select their prescription drug coverage for the coming year. Day encouraged people to begin comparing their options well before the deadline rather than risk leaving important decisions until the last minute.
